new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand description says Ana Tinga is a two-tone (H/L) language; it says nothing at all about word stress or accent, so no stress placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole phonology section is flagged by the authors as tentative (one-shot wordlist elicitation, 3 and 5 March 2005).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone only; no discussion of word- or phrase-level prominence, citation forms, or intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench & Douyon 2005 describe the speech of the single village Ana (Anana; ánà; 14 40.2 N, 3 07.1 W, Koro cercle), self-named Ana Tiŋa. Hochstetler et al. 2004 list this village under Yanda Dom, and Heath 2017 (p. 4) reports that his Yanda Dom consultants regard Ana village as Yanda Dom-speaking (yand1257) while Blench treats it as a distinct lect; Heath did no fieldwork there. Any proxy use of the Yanda Dom grammar for anat1248 should carry this caveat.

sources.note: Not a description of Ana: p. 2 lists Ana (Anana, ánà) among Yanda-zone villages; p. 4 sec. 1.5.1: Yanda assistants consider Ana village YD-speaking, Blench treats it as a distinct lect, and 'To date I have done no fieldwork on the Ana variety.' For Yanda Dom itself: tone language (ch. 3.7), no stress/accent section; 3.1.2 'Metrical structure' (p. 13) says medial syllable of CvCvCv may be metrically weak; incidental remark p. 217 on 'stress attack on the first syllable of H.H.H and of L.L.L words'.
